question: It takes \(A\) algebra books (all the same thickness) and \(H\) geometry books (all the same thickness, which is greater than that of an algebra book) to completely fill a certain shelf. Also, \(S\) of the algebra books and \(M\) of the geometry books would fill the same shelf. Finally, \(E\) of the algebra books alone would fill this shelf. Given that \(A,\) \(H,\) \(S,\) \(M,\) \(E\) are distinct positive integers, it follows that \(E\) is
solution:
Use the thickness of one algebra book as the unit of length, and let \(r>1\) be the thickness of a geometry book in these units. Since \(E\) algebra books fill the shelf, its length is \(E\) units. The two mixed arrangements therefore give
\[
A+Hr=E,\qquad S+Mr=E.
\]
We want \(E\), so eliminate the unknown thickness \(r\). Multiply the first equation by \(M\) and the second by \(H\):
\[
AM+HMr=ME,
\qquad SH+HMr=HE.
\]
Subtracting cancels the geometry-book contribution and gives
\[
AM-SH=(M-H)E.
\]
The integers \(M\) and \(H\) are distinct, so \(M-H\ne0\). Hence
\[
\boxed{E=\frac{AM-SH}{M-H}},
\]
choice \(\text{D}\).
